query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, thermal expansion mismatch between the matrix and coherent nanoprecipitates (or phase boundaries) produces internal residual stresses during cooling and thermal cycling that modulate dislocation dynamics. These internal stresses provide a unified mechanism for the observed high-temperature tensile creep behavior, cold-rolling microhardness changes, elastic modulus variations, and aging-induced hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized HfNbTaTiZr alloy produced by vacuum arc melting, HIP at ~1200 °C, and prolonged annealing designed to yield a uniform FCC or BCC matrix with the potential for coherent nanoprecipitate formation.
generation.intervention: Varying the thermal treatment post-synthesis by comparing a slow-cooled (minimizing thermal stress) versus a rapid-quenched or thermally cycled condition (maximizing thermal expansion mismatch induced stresses).
generation.conditions: Testing should span from room temperature up to high temperatures (~1250 °C) to cover: (1) high-temperature tensile creep tests, (2) microhardness measurements after cold rolling at ambient conditions, and (3) aging treatments in the 600–800 °C range to evolve precipitate populations. The baseline is the slow-cooled state with minimal residual thermal stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates or phase boundaries with differing thermal expansion coefficients relative to the primary matrix.
generation.mechanism: Upon cooling or during thermal cycling, differences in the thermal contraction of the matrix and precipitates generate internal residual stresses. These stresses alter dislocation mobility (by changing stacking-fault energies and dislocation pinning conditions) and influence phase stability, thereby affecting creep rates, yield strength, elastic moduli, and hardening behaviors during aging.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples processed with rapid quenching or intentional thermal cycling (thus with larger induced thermal residual stresses) will display higher yield strengths, enhanced high-temperature creep resistance, and altered elastic moduli compared to slow-cooled samples. Aging treatments should further accentuate these differences as additional nanoprecipitate evolution reinforces internal stress fields.
generation.baseline: Slow-cooled samples that minimize internal thermal stresses due to near-equilibrium cooling and reduced thermal expansion mismatch effects.
generation.boundary: The predicted residual stress effects will be most measurable at temperatures above ~600 °C (impacting creep and aging responses) and within the elastic modulus tests conducted between room temperature and 1100 K; below room temperature, the influence is expected to be minimal.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of thermal expansion mismatch is supported by disparate observations in similar systems, the quantitative contribution of the induced residual stresses to each mechanical property (tensile creep rate, microhardness, and elastic modulus) remains uncertain and will require detailed microstructural and stress mapping studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples using identical synthesis and HIP processing. For one group, apply a controlled slow-cooling protocol from 1200 °C to room temperature; for the other, apply a rapid-quenching or thermal cycling treatment to enhance thermal residual stresses. Subject both groups to identical tests: high-temperature tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness after cold rolling, and elastic modulus measurements from room temperature up to 1100 K. Characterize the residual stress state and nanoprecipitate distribution using X-ray diffraction and TEM.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and creep rate at 1250 °C
Elastic modulus across the 293–1100 K range
Residual stress levels measured by XRD
Nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and coherency via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid-quench (or thermally cycled) samples do not exhibit statistically significant differences in tensile creep behavior, microhardness, elastic modulus, or residual stress levels compared to the slow-cooled specimens, then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch induced residual stresses govern the unified stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior is falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.
